relations.evidence: The document update will be rejected with an HTTP 403 "Forbidden" error code, with the value of the forbidden: property being the HTTP status message.This is the preferred way to reject an update.

notable_absence.finding: This page is the primitive underneath requireAccess()/requireUser()/requireRole()'s shared 'signals rejection by throwing an exception' language elsewhere in this batch (see those pages' own findings): throw() IS the generic JS exception mechanism, and this page states its own preferred usage pattern is throw({forbidden: "..."}) specifically - a structured argument that becomes the HTTP 403 response's message, distinct from a require*() call's bare, no-payload throw. The page never states whether require*()'s internal throw also produces an HTTP 403, or a different code (e.g. 401) - so while the shared mechanism (JS throw) is confirmed, the shared RESPONSE CODE across all five rejection-capable calls (throw/requireAccess/requireUser/requireRole/requireAdmin) is not stated anywhere in this batch and is left an open question for reconciliation rather than assumed.

cross_component_finding: The Context section frames throw() as the general-purpose validation/rejection primitive ('You enforce the validity of document structure by checking the necessary constraints and throwing an exception if they're not met'), with the require*() family - documented on the other seven pages in this batch - as convenience wrappers that check one specific, common condition (a channel grant, a role, a specific user, or the Admin API surface) and throw on the caller's behalf. The page also recommends against relying on server-side validation as the primary safeguard ('The server-side sync function validation should be seen as a fail-safe and a guard against malicious access'), and introduces the oldDoc/doc distinction (also emphasized independently on requireUser()'s own page in this batch) as the mechanism for comparing a new revision against the prior one to detect illegal state changes.
